facts.statement: The genus Allognathosuchus was named in 1921.
Allognathosuchus was a medium-sized predator reaching up to 1.5 meters in length.
facts.quote: Allognathosuchus was a medium-sized predator up to 1.5 m in length.

facts.statement: Allognathosuchus possessed stout jaws and bulbous teeth located near the rear of both the upper and lower jaw tooth rows.
facts.quote: This alligatorine is known for its stout jaws and bulbous teeth, found near the rear of the tooth row in upper and lower jaws.

facts.statement: Historically, the stout jaws and bulbous teeth of Allognathosuchus have been interpreted as adaptations for crushing mollusks.
facts.quote: These adaptations have historically been interpreted as having been for crushing mollusks.

facts.statement: The species A. polyodon, A. heterodon, and A. wartheni lived during the Clarkforkian, Wasatchian, and Bridgerian North American Land Mammal Ages.
facts.quote: A. polyodon, A. heterodon, and A. wartheni span the Clarkforkian, Wasatchian, and Bridgerian North American Land Mammal Ages.

facts.statement: Allognathosuchus lived from the Campanian to the Priabonian stages, between 83.6 and 33.9 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Priabonian (83.6 to 33.9 million years ago)

facts.statement: Allognathosuchus is an extinct genus of alligatorine crocodylians, with the name meaning "other jaw crocodile".
facts.quote: Allognathosuchus (meaning "other jaw crocodile") is an extinct genus of alligatorine crocodylian

facts.statement: Allognathosuchus is classified within the subfamily Alligatorinae and the family Alligatoridae.
While recent studies consistently place A. polyodon and A. wartheni within Alligatorinae, their exact relative placement within the group remains disputed.
facts.quote: Recent studies have consistently resolved Allognathosuchus polyodon and Allognathosuchus wartheni as members of Alligatorinae, although their relative placement is disputed

facts.statement: In 2004, Christopher Brochu reviewed the genus and recommended its conservative use due to the fragmentary nature of the remains for several species.
facts.quote: Christopher Brochu reviewed the genus in 2004, and in light of the fragmentary remains of several of the species involved, recommended conservative use of the genus.
